title: Lottery Winners Who Went Broke: What Really Happened
description: Jack Whittaker. Evelyn Adams. Willie Hurt. These lottery winners had millions — then didn't. Here's what the documented record actually shows.
content:
The Day the Money Arrived — and the Clock Started Ticking

For most people, the fantasy ends at the ticket counter. You check the numbers, let yourself imagine for a moment, and then go back to whatever you were doing before. But for a small group of Americans, the numbers actually matched. The money arrived. And for some of them, that arrival set in motion a sequence of events nobody had prepared for — not the winners, not their families, and not the financial systems meant to support them.

The stories of lottery winners who went broke tend to get reduced to cautionary punchlines: they won millions and ended up with nothing. But the documented record is more complicated, more human, and more worth understanding than that framing suggests. These are real people — with real lives before the ticket and real consequences after it — and their stories deserve to be told with the care and specificity the facts allow.

Who They Were Before the Win

Jack Whittaker: Already Successful, Still Searching

Jack Whittaker of Putnam County, West Virginia, was not the archetypal struggling lottery dreamer. By December 2002, he was the president of a construction company and reportedly already worth several million dollars on his own. He played the lottery as a habit, not a lifeline. On Christmas Day 2002, that habit produced something extraordinary: a ticket matching all five numbers plus the Powerball in a drawing that had rolled for weeks.

What Whittaker held was a $314.9 million Powerball jackpot — the largest single-ticket jackpot in U.S. lottery history at that time. He was a churchgoing man who publicly pledged a tithe to Christian charities and spoke at the press conference about gratitude. The portrait was of a grounded person who might, just maybe, be equipped to handle what was coming.

Evelyn Adams: Two Wins, One Outcome

Evelyn Adams of New Jersey accomplished something that statistically borders on the impossible: she won the New Jersey Lottery not once but twice — in 1985 and again in 1986 — for a combined total of $5.4 million. Before those wins, she was working at a store and described her life as ordinary. The double win made national headlines and turned her into a symbol of improbable fortune.

Adams was by most accounts generous to a fault. She gave money to friends and family freely, and she was drawn to the Atlantic City casinos, where she gambled heavily. The combination of open-handed giving and sustained losses at the tables proved to be more than the winnings could absorb.

Willie Hurt: A Win That Arrived at the Wrong Moment

Willie Hurt won $3.1 million in the Michigan Lottery in 1989. Before the win, Hurt was a man with a family and a life that, by his own later account, was already under significant strain. The lottery win did not resolve those strains. According to court documents cited in published reports, Hurt developed a serious crack cocaine addiction in the period following his win, and within approximately two years the money was largely gone. By 1991 he was facing murder charges, a trajectory that reporters and researchers have since cited repeatedly when documenting what can follow a sudden windfall for someone already in crisis.

The Moment of the Claim — Announcements, Lump Sums, and First Decisions

Whittaker took his $314.9 million jackpot as a lump sum, which after federal and state taxes left him with a cash payout widely reported at approximately $113 million. He made charitable donations publicly and quickly, establishing the Jack Whittaker Foundation to fund scholarships and provide food and clothing to rural West Virginia families. It was a genuinely substantive philanthropic commitment, not a photo-opportunity gesture. But the public announcement of his wealth also opened a door he could not close.

Adams' two wins were paid as annuities under the lottery structures of the mid-1980s, spreading the $5.4 million over time rather than delivering it as a single lump sum. That structure might theoretically have provided a buffer — but the documented pattern of giving and gambling accelerated faster than the payments arrived. The Longer Arc — How the Money Moved and Where It Went

In Whittaker's case, the money moved in several directions at once and not all of them were chosen freely. He was robbed twice — once of $545,000 in cash taken from his car outside a strip club, according to news reports, and again in a separate incident. He faced a series of civil lawsuits, some related to bounced checks at casinos where he had reportedly been gambling heavily himself. His granddaughter Brandi, whom he had described as the person he most wanted to provide for, died in 2004 under circumstances reported as a drug overdose. The grief that followed, by his own documented accounts, was the wound that no amount of money could address. "I wish I'd torn that ticket up," Whittaker was quoted as saying in multiple subsequent interviews.

For Evelyn Adams, the arc was quieter but no less complete. Published accounts from the 2000s described her as living in a trailer, a detail she discussed openly in interviews. She told reporters she did not regret the generosity — the giving was consistent with who she was — but acknowledged the gambling losses as decisions she would revisit. New Jersey lottery history includes Adams as one of its most documented winners, for reasons that extend well beyond the double-win improbability.

Willie Hurt's documented timeline was the most compressed. The combination of addiction, family breakdown, and legal trouble collapsed a $3.1 million windfall into crisis within roughly two years. Court documents, not tabloid speculation, established the timeline and the contributing factors. His case has been cited in academic and policy discussions about lottery winner support structures, or the lack of them.

The Most Human Moment in the Record

"I wish I'd torn that ticket up." — Jack Whittaker, in multiple documented interviews following the deaths of family members and the loss of his fortune, as reported by the Associated Press and other outlets.

That sentence, stripped of everything else, contains the full weight of what the documented record shows. Whittaker did not say he wished he'd managed the money better, or hired better advisors, or made different investments. He wished the win had never happened. From a man who had already been a millionaire before Christmas 2002, that statement is worth sitting with.

What the Documented Patterns Reveal

Researchers and financial planners who study lottery winners — including studies published by the National Bureau of Economic Research — have found that sudden large windfalls do not automatically produce financial stability, and in some cases accelerate existing vulnerabilities. The stories of lottery winners who went broke are not random or inexplicable; they tend to cluster around a few recognizable dynamics: the rapid expansion of social demands and requests from family and community, a lack of existing infrastructure for managing large sums, and pre-existing personal struggles that money cannot resolve and may in fact intensify.

None of that makes these outcomes inevitable or predictable. Plenty of jackpot winners — including Mavis Wanczyk, who won $758.7 million in 2017 and quietly stepped out of public life, and Merle and Patricia Butler, who waited months before claiming their $218.6 million Mega Millions share in 2012 — have navigated their wins without documented financial collapse. The difference, where it can be traced, often has more to do with circumstances and support systems than with the size of the check. What the record doesn't support is the simple morality tale — the idea that these people were foolish or careless in ways that most people would have avoided. Grief, addiction, exploitation, and the social pressure that descends on a publicly known winner are not character flaws. They are forces that most people have never had to face at the scale that a nine-figure jackpot announcement creates.
